name: Retrosynthesis
tagline: Working backwards from target to starting materials — the logic of synthesis.
seo_title: Retrosynthesis — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Retrosynthesis on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in synthesis planning, disconnection strategy and AI-driven retrosynthesis.

definition.lead: Retrosynthesis plans a synthesis backwards: start from the target molecule and cut it into simpler pieces until you reach materials you can buy.
definition.body: Formalized by E. J. Corey in the 1960s, it turned synthesis planning from intuition into logic. Today computer programs and AI models search huge numbers of possible disconnections and suggest routes in seconds.

facts.label: the retrosynthetic arrow, meaning 'can be made from'
Corey sets out the logic of retrosynthetic analysis
Corey receives the Nobel Prize in Chemistry

branches.name: Disconnections

branches.example: Cutting the C–C bond next to a carbonyl group.

branches.name: Functional group interconversion

branches.name: Strategic bonds
branches.summary: Choosing the cuts that simplify the most.
branches.example: Disconnecting rings and branch points first.

branches.example: From LHASA (1969) to today's commercial planners.

timeline.title: Thinking backwards
timeline.text: Robert Robinson's tropinone synthesis reflects a backward analysis of the target.
timeline.why: An early example of retrosynthetic logic.

timeline.title: Corey's logic
timeline.text: E. J. Corey publishes general methods for planning the synthesis of complex molecules.
timeline.why: Turned intuition into a teachable method.

timeline.title: LHASA
timeline.text: Corey and Todd Wipke describe computer-assisted synthesis design.

timeline.title: The disconnection approach
timeline.text: Stuart Warren publishes a textbook built around disconnections.

timeline.title: The Logic of Chemical Synthesis
timeline.text: Corey and Xue-Min Cheng publish their book on synthesis strategy.
timeline.why: A reference for generations of synthetic chemists.

timeline.title: Nobel Prize
timeline.text: Corey is awarded the Nobel Prize for the theory and methodology of organic synthesis.
timeline.why: Retrosynthesis recognized at the highest level.

timeline.title: Networks of reactions
timeline.text: Bartosz Grzybowski's team reports progress with Chematica, an expert synthesis planner.
timeline.why: Showed computers could plan non-trivial routes.

timeline.title: Deep learning plans syntheses
timeline.text: Marwin Segler, Mike Preuss and Mark Waller combine neural networks with tree search.
timeline.why: AI routes judged comparable to literature routes by chemists.

timeline.title: Reactions as translation
timeline.text: The Molecular Transformer predicts reaction outcomes like a language model.

quiz.q: What does the retrosynthetic arrow ⇒ mean?
quiz.explain: It points from the target to its precursors.

options: An idealized fragment produced by a disconnection
A real reagent bought from a supplier
A solvent chosen for the reaction
A catalyst that speeds up the step
quiz.explain: It may not exist as such: a 'carbanion' synthon is supplied by a real reagent.

quiz.q: The real reagent that stands in for a synthon is called…
quiz.explain: For example, a Grignard reagent for a carbanion synthon.
Changing a group on paper so a good disconnection becomes possible.

quiz.q: Who formalized retrosynthesis and won the 1990 Nobel Prize?
quiz.explain: He also designed many reagents and named reactions.
Every paper cut must be a reaction you can actually run forwards.

quiz.q: Disconnecting a C–C bond next to a carbonyl often points to…
options: An enolate alkylation or aldol reaction
quiz.explain: The carbon next to a carbonyl can act as a nucleophile through its enolate.

quiz.q: A Diels–Alder retrosynthesis cuts which kind of ring?
quiz.explain: Recognizing a cyclohexene suggests a diene plus a dienophile.

options: An early computer program for synthesis planning
A reaction named after its inventor
A catalyst used in total synthesis
quiz.explain: Developed by Corey and Wipke at Harvard.

quiz.q: Why plan backwards instead of forwards?
options: The target is fixed, so working back narrows a huge space of options to logical cuts
Forward planning is not allowed in synthesis
It saves solvent in the laboratory
quiz.explain: From any starting material, the forward possibilities explode.

quiz.q: The Molecular Transformer (2019) treats reaction prediction like…
options: Translating reactant SMILES into product SMILES
quiz.explain: The same architecture as machine translation.

quiz.q: Why is a convergent route often preferred?
options: Overall yield drops less than in one long linear sequence
It is always cheaper than a linear route
quiz.explain: Fewer steps lie on the longest path to the target.
